newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco approves United Airlines lease.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco approves United Airlines lease.

text.p: San Francisco's Board of Supervisors approved a United Airlines' lease at San Francisco airport Monday after the two sides compromised on whether the airline must offer benefits to unmarried partners of its employees.
The city's governing board voted 9-0 to approve United's two-year lease on a new ground equipment repair facility and flight kitchen at San Francisco International Airport, supervisors said.
UAL Corp's United Airlines has an option to extend the lease for another 23 years, but to do so, it must comply with a domestic partners' ordinance passed late last year by the Board of Supervisors.

The citywide ordinance requires companies doing business with San Francisco to provide the same benefits they provide to spouses to employees' unmarried partners, whether gay or heterosexual. The law covers benefits such as bereavement leave, medical leave and health insurance.
The Board of Supervisors had delayed approving the 25-year lease United was originally seeking, saying they wanted the airline to comply with the domestic partners law.

The airline objected, saying the new law does not take effect until June and that the condition had not been mentioned during negotiations on the lease last year, news reports said. Another issue was whether it had to offer the benefits nationwide or worldwide, not just in San Francisco.

United Airlines, the biggest carrier at San Francisco airport, does not currently extend benefits to domestic partners in the United States. Some large companies do offer benefits to domestic partners.

Supervisor Leslie Katz, a co-author of the domestic partners law, said she was "thrilled" by the agreement with United Airlines. "We've gotten every indication from United that they are moving toward compliance with the ordinance," she said.

While United Airlines has not publicly committed itself to extending benefits to domestic partners, supervisors said they were confident it would do so because it would not want to walk away from the investment it was making in the new facilities at San Francisco airport.

Larry Clark, vice president, property and facilities, for United Airlines, said the company was pleased the board had approved the lease. He said the agreement would give United time to fully review the domestic partners' ordinance.
United Airlines said it was engaged in a comprehensive analysis of the ordinance, including the tax, finance, human resources, benefits, labor relations and legal ramifications of implementing it.
